pages_convention: Mixed. XML section and paragraph locators (jats_text) for the abstract (§0 ¶1) and caption labels as printed (e.g. Fig. 3). Printed journal pages (pp. 64-83, PDF page 1 = p. 64) for body text, because the supplied XML file holds no body text.

entry.evidence: the parameters that control the emergence of laminations vary between elements and tend to be multi-factorial

sequences.source_document: Published paper (PDF) with XML abstract and captions

steps.action: Pose the question of what controls Sr and Y co-variation and fluorescent laminations in active and fossil stalagmites from La Vallina cave.
steps.quote: with a particular focus on strontium and yttrium co-variations and fluorescent laminations

steps.action: Adopt the classical hypothesis that Sr incorporation increases with growth rate (Lorens 1981) and the earlier conceptual model of Sr as a soluble and Y as a colloidally transported element.
steps.quote: We begin by testing the classical notion that Sr incorporation is positively driven by growth rate

steps.action: Combine confocal fluorescence imaging, LA-ICP-MS transects, georeferencing and a MATLAB script that estimates growth rate and a PCP-corrected DSr from coeval Mg/Ca; add wavelet coherence and a moving Pearson correlation.
steps.quote: A MATLAB script was written to allow for semi-automated estimation of growth rate and associated trace element concentrations

steps.action: Check LA-ICP-MS precision against the NIST610 glass standard and assess reproducibility qualitatively with parallel transects.
steps.quote: Additional parallel transects were obtained to gain a qualitative assessment of the reproducibility of the method.

steps.action: Use drip water monitoring data from La Vallina (Sr/Ca, Y, drip rates), published by the group in Kost et al. (2022).
steps.quote: Drip water data from La Vallina demonstrate two key points.

steps.action: Estimate drip-water-based DSr (0.07-0.09; GUI 0.19), yearly Y delivery, Y deposition and the deposition/delivery trapping efficiency for each drip site.
steps.quote: estimates for DSr can be obtained which range between 0.07 and 0.09

steps.action: Measure F14C by AMS in the active stalagmites and find modern carbon and a bomb-spike peak.
steps.quote: a distinct peak corresponding to the acceleration and subsequent cessation of atmospheric nuclear arms testing

steps.action: Infer average growth rates of the active stalagmites (about 70-320 µm/yr) by setting the bomb-spike base to 1959; take fossil growth rates from published U-Th dates.
steps.quote: The location of the base of this peak (1959 CE) allows for growth rate estimates

steps.action: Image fluorescence patterns: distinct layering in fossil stalagmites; ambiguous or sub-annual banding in most active stalagmites.
steps.quote: Distinct fluorescent layering is most prominent in fossil stalagmites

steps.action: Check that fluorescent layers in GUI are annual by counting 55 peaks between the collection date and the independently dated bomb-spike base.
steps.quote: comparison with the location of the 14C bomb spike base (1959) confirms that these layers are, for the most part, seasonal

steps.action: Establish across stalagmites that bright fluorescent bands coincide with Y peaks, with rare exceptions.
steps.quote: a close correspondence between bright fluorescent peaks and Y

steps.action: Compare the growth-rate hypothesis with GEL and GAR data: regress 100-layer average growth rate against Sr/Ca, Sr/Mg and DSr (R2 0.1-0.3, mixed significance).
steps.quote: GEL shows a significant correlation between growth rate and Sr/Mg and DSr

steps.action: Repeat the DSr-growth rate test with growth rates from trace element cycles in three other stalagmites (GAL, GAE, GUI), on a seasonal scale.
steps.quote: A similar effect can be demonstrated on a seasonal scale using trace element variations

steps.action: Record a weak negative relation between Y/Ca and growth rate in GEL, GAR, GAE and GUI, and a slight positive one in GAL.
steps.quote: a weak negative relationship with growth rate is observed in GEL and GAR

steps.action: Establish persistent Sr-Y anti-correlation in fossil stalagmites at annual, decadal and centennial scales, using wavelet coherence and moving Pearson correlation.
steps.quote: wherein large negative Sr excursions are most often associated with simultaneous positive Y excursions

steps.action: Observe irregular Sr-Y behaviour in four active stalagmites, and in GUI a loss of anti-correlation about 20 years before collection, with Sr/Ca rising and δ13C and δ18O excursions.
steps.quote: GUI is notable in that the previously strong Sr-Y anti-correlation diminishes about 20 years before the collection date

steps.action: Support the assumption of no exogenous detrital Sr with the negative Sr-Al correlation in all datasets (Fig. S10).
steps.quote: the generally negative correlation between Sr and Al in all datasets

steps.action: Check the new PCP-corrected DSr estimates (Rayleigh correction from minimum Mg/Ca) against drip-water-derived coefficients and literature values.
steps.quote: measured distribution coefficients (Table 2) as well as literature values

steps.action: Introduce the rival that solution supersaturation, rather than growth rate itself, controls DSr (Wasylenki et al. 2005).
steps.quote: suggest that solution supersaturation is actually the dominant factor controlling both growth rate and DSr

steps.action: Run I-STAL for two soil pCO2 scenarios to show that the saturation-dependent DSr-growth rate relation shifts slope and intercept.
steps.quote: Forward modeling allows for the illustration of how this relationship may vary

steps.action: Split the GAR DSr-growth rate data into top and bottom segments across Termination II and find two distinct, more significant regressions.
steps.quote: yields two distinct regressions, each more significant than the regression over the entire dataset

steps.action: Reconcile the claim with farming experiments that found no Sr-growth rate relation by questioning their auxiliaries (unseeded plates, ACC phase, mass-based versus extension growth rate).
steps.quote: stalagmite growth/farming experiments have not demonstrated this relationship

steps.action: Take up the rival that Y peaks record heavy autumnal infiltration, i.e. organic flux (Borsato et al. 2007).
steps.quote: led Borsato et al. (2007) to speculate that Y was recording the delivery of heavy autumnal infiltration in the cave

steps.action: Set flux as the primary control aside: stalagmite Y varies by orders of magnitude within a year while drip water Y varies by about one.
steps.quote: most likely controlled by crystallization processes rather than flux

steps.action: Propose a three-effect conceptual model for Y incorporation (retention, dilation, delivery), with delivery subordinate.
steps.quote: we propose a model to explain Y variation in stalagmites based on three overlapping effects

steps.action: Compare retention with Y deposition/delivery versus drip rate at five sites (Fig. 11, R2 0.50, p 0.09), and dilation with the long-term Sr-Y anti-correlation (Fig. 8).
steps.quote: stalagmites under faster drips retain less of the delivered Y

steps.action: Exclude regional air temperature, the Suess effect and PCP change as causes of the GUI excursion, using SNO and other active stalagmites as references.
steps.quote: also rules out the Suess effect, which would affect all stalagmites

steps.action: State three rival explanations for the recent GUI Sr-Y change: eucalyptus land-use change, reduced autumnal rainfall or P-ET, and Y dilation by faster growth.
steps.quote: recent Sr-Y systematics can be explained in several ways

steps.action: Weaken the rainfall explanation (earlier precipitation changes of similar size left no Sr signal) and the P-ET variant (inconsistent with fast growth).
steps.quote: similar to changes in prior decades which are not associated with a sudden Sr increase in GUI

steps.action: Test dilation in GUI: Y/Ca halves as growth rate rises from about 138 to 220 µm/yr, making dilation plausible.
steps.quote: The dilation effect can be tested in a simple way by examining the average Y/Ca over intervals of variable growth rate.

steps.action: Ask whether an explanation without eucalyptus exists, since fossil stalagmites show similar Sr excursions; sketch root-system and feeding-fracture alternatives.
steps.quote: is there an alternate explanation for the preceding trends that excludes eucalyptus altogether?

steps.action: Against DOM inhibition of Sr (Borsato et al. 2007), propose that Sr-Y anti-correlation arises indirectly from ventilation, drip rate and solution chemistry acting on each element.
steps.quote: the correlation may be indirectly linked to the complex interplay between cave ventilation, drip rate and solution chemistry

steps.action: Refine the model: poor Sr-Y anti-correlation in active stalagmites with summer drips implies that such periods mark increased summer dripping.
steps.quote: represent times of increased summer drip rate

steps.action: Test with a synthetic averaging exercise (Fig. S7) that laser averaging over condensed layers does not inflate mean Y.
steps.quote: averaging across several layers of variable thickness but with constant amplitude merely results in a lower-amplitude measured signal

steps.action: Keep the conceptual Sr-Y incorporation model (Fig. 13) as an interpretation, possibly specific to La Vallina.
steps.quote: The conceptual model for Sr-Y incorporation is summarized in Fig. 13

end.claim: Persistent Sr-Y anti-correlation in La Vallina stalagmites is best explained by an interplay in which DSr rises with growth rate (driven by supersaturation and cave ventilation) while Y, delivered by colloids, is controlled by surface retention time, dilation and drip water flux.

decisive_move.sentence: Establishing, with coupled LA-ICP-MS and confocal imaging across many stalagmites, that Sr and Y are persistently anti-correlated and that Y peaks coincide with fluorescent bands is what the conceptual model explains.

gates.evidence: Action: the growth-rate hypothesis directed the layer-counted segment analysis (p. 65), but samples were mostly naturally broken and collected earlier (p. 65). Claim: the DSr-growth regressions could have failed and returned modest but significant fits (p. 69); the Y model is supported only qualitatively, with Fig. 11 at p = 0.09 on five sites. Registration: nothing is reported as fixed before the data were seen.

novelty_claims.quote: we employ a novel method of estimating DSr
we focus on Sr and Y and derive novel interpretations based on their covariations

limits: The supplied XML contains only the abstract and captions, so body steps cite printed pages; the supplement (Figs. S1-S10, PCP correction, MATLAB code) was not supplied. Sub-claims at other statuses: annual fluorescent banding is confirmed, but only in GUI against the 14C bomb spike (p. 68); the DSr-growth rate relation is regularity_in_range (R2 0.1-0.3 across stalagmites, analysis restricted to growth >60 µm/yr, p. 78); DSr values are estimate_with_resolution in range only, as no uncertainties are given and the authors say they should be treated with caution (p. 76); the retention model rests on five drip sites with p = 0.09 (Fig. 11); the GUI excursion is left among unresolved rivals (pp. 79-80). Inference: the samples were collected before the hypotheses were posed, so the hypothesis did not direct acquisition. No test in other caves is performed (p. 80). The Fig. 12 caption cites Fig. 4 for GAR data, apparently meaning Fig. 5. No review file, so no review sequence is coded.

disagreements.target: Tremaine and Froelich (2013); Wassenburg et al. (2020) farming experiments
disagreements.support: The authors argue that unseeded plates, a possible ACC phase and mass-based growth rates may explain the absent Sr-growth relation; they offer no new experiment.
disagreements.quote: stalagmite growth/farming experiments have not demonstrated this relationship

disagreements.target: Studies interpreting Sr maxima as fast growth (Lorens 1981; Baker et al. 2014; Belli et al. 2017; Borsato et al. [...]
disagreements.support: They correct Sr/Ca for PCP using coeval Mg/Ca before relating DSr to growth rate.
disagreements.quote: However, because Sr concentration is also a function of PCP, we employ a novel method of estimating DSr.

disagreements.target: Borsato et al. (2007): Y records heavy autumnal infiltration
disagreements.support: Drip water Y varies by about one order of magnitude while stalagmite Y varies by several, citing Baldini et al. (2012) and Fairchild et al. (2010).
disagreements.quote: The connection of this effect to seasonal Y peaks in stalagmites is, however, difficult.

disagreements.target: Borsato et al. (2007): fluorescent banding from organic flushing from soil
disagreements.support: They propose instead autumnal optimal depositional conditions based on adsorption/desorption kinetics; the argument is conceptual.
disagreements.quote: they interpret the banding as the result of organic flushing from the soil as opposed to autumnal optimal depositional conditions described here

disagreements.target: Borsato et al. (2007): Sr incorporation inhibited by high DOM flux
disagreements.support: They offer an indirect explanation through ventilation, drip rate and dilation, illustrated by the active stalagmites.
disagreements.quote: Alternately, the correlation may be indirectly linked to the complex interplay between cave ventilation, drip rate and solution chemistry

alternatives_considered.reason: Laser integration of thin layers smooths the signal, so low amplitudes would correlate with slow growth

alternatives_considered.chosen: Run the ICP-MS mostly without the collision/reaction cell
Treat the GAR top and bottom segments separately
alternatives_considered.alternatives: A single regression over the whole dataset
alternatives_considered.reason: Shifting climatic conditions across Termination II, following Belli et al. (2017)

alternatives_considered.chosen: 'Partition coefficient' for Sr and 'incorporation' for Y

alternatives_considered.reason: All Sr is assumed fluid-derived and substituted for Ca; Y has complex partitioning and low solubility
